title: Beginner Swahili
summary: Start speaking Kiswahili: greetings and courtesy, pronunciation and numbers, noun classes and agreement, building verbs with subject, tense and object markers, Swahili time and days, and everyday conversations.
audience: Complete beginners, students, travellers and professionals working in East and Central Africa

body.p: Swahili (Kiswahili) is spoken by tens of millions of people in East and Central Africa as a first or second language. It is a national or official language in Tanzania, Kenya, Uganda and Rwanda, widely used in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and an official language of the African Union and the East African Community. It is a Bantu language with many words from Arabic and other languages.

list: Habari? / Habari yako?: How are you? (literally "what news?"). Reply: Nzuri (good), or Salama (peaceful).
Habari za asubuhi?: Good morning (news of the morning?).
Hujambo? (to one person): How are you? Reply: Sijambo (I am fine).
Jambo: a simple hello, common with visitors.
Shikamoo: a respectful greeting to an elder; the elder replies Marahaba.
Mambo? / Vipi?: informal greetings among young people. Reply: Poa (cool, fine).
Asante (sana): thank you (very much). Karibu: welcome, you're welcome.
Tafadhali: please. Samahani: sorry, excuse me.
Kwa heri: goodbye (to one person); Kwa herini: goodbye (to several).
Jina langu ni Baraka: My name is Baraka. Jina lako nani?: What is your name?

body.tip: Greetings matter in Swahili-speaking cultures; take time to greet before asking for anything.

list: Swahili spelling is very regular; words are pronounced as written.
Five vowels: a (as in "father"), e (as in "bed"), i (as in "see"), o (as in "more"), u (as in "too").
Stress is almost always on the second-last syllable: ki-TA-bu, ha-BA-ri.
Every vowel is pronounced: "kaa" (sit, stay) has two a sounds.
ng' (with an apostrophe) sounds like the ng in "singer": ng'ombe (cow).

body.p: 1 moja, 2 mbili, 3 tatu, 4 nne, 5 tano, 6 sita, 7 saba, 8 nane, 9 tisa, 10 kumi. Teens use na (and): 11 kumi na moja, 15 kumi na tano. Tens: 20 ishirini, 30 thelathini, 40 arobaini, 50 hamsini, 60 sitini, 70 sabini, 80 themanini, 90 tisini, 100 mia moja. Many of the higher numbers come from Arabic.
Prices: Ni bei gani? / Bei gani? (How much is it?) Shilingi mia mbili (two hundred shillings).

body.tip: Practise numbers with prices at the market or in shops; they become automatic quickly.

body.p: Like other Bantu languages, Swahili groups nouns into classes, each with prefixes for singular and plural. The class also changes the form of adjectives and verbs that agree with the noun, which is the key to Swahili grammar.

list: M-WA class (people): mtoto, watoto (child, children); mwalimu, walimu (teacher, teachers); mtu, watu (person, people).
M-MI class (trees, plants, some objects): mti, miti (tree, trees); mji, miji (town, towns).
KI-VI class (many things and tools): kitabu, vitabu (book, books); kiti, viti (chair, chairs).
JI-MA class (various): jicho, macho (eye, eyes); gari, magari (car, cars).
N class (many animals and loan words): same form for singular and plural: ndizi (banana, bananas), simba (lion, lions).
U class (abstract ideas and some objects): uhuru (freedom), upendo (love).

body.p: Adjectives take the class prefix: mtoto mzuri (a good child), watoto wazuri (good children), kitabu kizuri (a good book), vitabu vizuri (good books). The adjective root -zuri stays the same; the prefix changes.

body.tip: Learn nouns in singular-plural pairs (kitabu/vitabu); the pair shows you the class.

body.p: Swahili verbs are built from parts: subject prefix + tense marker + (object marker) + verb root. Once you know the parts, you can build many forms.
ni- (I), u- (you), a- (he/she), tu- (we), m- (you plural), wa- (they, people). There is no separate word for he and she.

list: -na- present: ninasoma (I am reading / I read), anasoma (she or he reads).
-li- past: nilisoma (I read, past), walisoma (they read).
-ta- future: nitasoma (I will read), tutasoma (we will read).
-me- perfect: nimesoma (I have read).

body.p: An object marker goes before the root: ninakupenda (ni-na-ku-penda) means "I love you"; ninamwona means "I see him or her". Negatives change the prefix and ending: sisomi (I don't read), hatusomi (we don't read); for the past, sikusoma (I didn't read).

body.tip: Take one verb root, such as -soma (read) or -kula (eat), and build it with every subject prefix and tense; patterns become clear fast.

body.p: Swahili time is counted from sunrise, about 6 a.m., so it is six hours different from the standard clock. Saa moja asubuhi (hour one in the morning) is 7 a.m.; saa sita mchana (hour six at midday) is 12 noon; saa moja usiku is 7 p.m. To convert, add or subtract six hours: 1 p.m. (13:00) is saa saba mchana. Saa ngapi? means "What time is it?"
Jumatatu (Monday), Jumanne (Tuesday), Jumatano (Wednesday), Alhamisi (Thursday), Ijumaa (Friday), Jumamosi (Saturday), Jumapili (Sunday).

list: Ninaitwa…: I am called…
Ninatoka Nigeria: I come from Nigeria.
Sielewi: I don't understand. Sema polepole, tafadhali: Speak slowly, please.
Choo kiko wapi?: Where is the toilet?
Nataka maji / chai / chakula: I want water / tea / food.
Pole: sorry (sympathy). Pole pole: slowly.

body.tip: When someone says a time in Swahili, check whether they mean Swahili time or the standard clock.

body.p: mama (mother), baba (father), kaka (brother), dada (sister), mtoto (child), bibi (grandmother), babu (grandfather), familia (family). Possessives agree with the noun class: mama yangu (my mother), kitabu changu (my book), vitabu vyangu (my books).

list: chakula (food), maji (water), chai (tea), wali (cooked rice), ugali (maize meal porridge), nyama (meat), samaki (fish), matunda (fruit).
Nataka kununua…: I want to buy…
Ni bei gani?: How much is it?
Punguza bei, tafadhali: Reduce the price, please.

body.p: A: Habari yako? B: Nzuri, asante. Na wewe? A: Salama. Jina lako nani? B: Jina langu ni Neema. Unatoka wapi? A: Ninatoka Ghana. B: Karibu sana Tanzania!

body.tip: Listen to Swahili radio or music; hearing natural speech daily builds comprehension quickly.
